title: Swiatek Triumphs in Toronto, Securing First Title of a Challenging Season
summary:
After months of struggle and criticism, Iga Swiatek finally has a trophy to celebrate. The six-time Grand Slam champion defeated world number two Elena Rybakina 6-2 6-3 in the Canadian Open final in Toronto on Thursday, securing her first WTA title of the season and her 26th career title. The match lasted just one hour and 15 minutes, with Swiatek, ranked eighth, breaking Rybakina's serve in the second set and winning five of the final six games after trailing 2-1.

"It means so, so much to me because the past months were not easy," Swiatek said after the match. The Polish star has had a turbulent season: she reached the quarter-finals of the Australian Open but lost to eventual champion Rybakina, and she only made it to the fourth round of the French Open and the third round of Wimbledon. In April, she added Francisco Roig—a former coach of Rafael Nadal and Emma Raducanu—to her team. Swiatek acknowledged the difficulty of dealing with external criticism while trying to find her best form. "I'm really happy that I kept focusing on growing, changing my game a little bit, improving despite all the opinions that many people have about me every day on the internet," she said. "It's not easy to deal with all of that."

Rybakina, who had won her previous three matches in three sets, struggled with consistency, hitting just 13 winners and making 23 unforced errors. "I tried my best but it wasn't enough," she said. Swiatek's victory was also brightened by a canine guest at the trophy ceremony, adding a lighthearted moment to her emotional win.

In other news, Britain's Katie Boulter earned her first career win at the Cincinnati Open, defeating Katie Volynets 7-5 0-6 6-4. She'll face Wimbledon champion Linda Noskova next. And in the men's final, Ben Shelton won his second consecutive Canadian Open title, beating fellow American Brandon Nakashima 6-3 7-6 (7-4). Shelton became the first player since Novak Djokovic in 2016 to win the tournament without dropping a set, and the first since Rafael Nadal in 2019 to successfully defend the title.
why_it_matters: Swiatek's win shows how elite athletes navigate public criticism while trying to improve, and it demonstrates that a single victory can shift momentum in a long season.

background_read: On the WTA (Women's Tennis Association) tour, the Canadian Open is one of the most established hard-court tournaments in North America, and this year's women's event was held in Toronto.
Iga Swiatek (a Polish tennis star and six-time Grand Slam champion) has experienced both dominance and pressure since her first major breakthrough at the French Open.

Elena Rybakina (the world number two and a Wimbledon champion from Kazakhstan) had already beaten Swiatek at the Australian Open earlier in the season, so the Toronto final felt like a chance for revenge.

Swiatek's decision to add Francisco Roig (a coach who previously worked with Rafael Nadal, a Spanish tennis great, and Emma Raducanu, a British Grand Slam champion) reflects how top players seek tactical change during rough patches.
The men's result also tapped into history: Ben Shelton's title run matched rare feats associated with Novak Djokovic, a Serbian all-time great, and Rafael Nadal.

perspectives.description: They see this title as proof that making tactical changes and ignoring internet criticism can pay off, restoring confidence after a difficult stretch.
They may point out that one title does not erase earlier losses, and the intense public scrutiny itself shows the heavy mental toll social media can take on athletes.
They note that Rybakina's 23 unforced errors and fatigue from previous three-set matches contributed heavily to the result, so one commanding win does not yet prove a full return to top form.

They will watch whether Swiatek can carry this momentum into the next big tournaments, and whether her new coaching partnership can help her handle both the technical and psychological demands of elite tennis.
